expected_correct_answer_summary: YES, decisively. Higher tobacco taxes/cigarette prices reduce smoking consumption and prevalence. WHO: +10% price → ~4% (HIC) / ~5% (LMIC) less consumption. Elasticity negative across income groups (~-0.36 HIC, -0.21 LMIC; Nargis et al. 2021). CPSTF (116 studies) 'strong evidence' recommendation: a 20% price increase cuts consumption 10.4%, adult prevalence 3.6%, youth initiation 8.6%. CDC: 'one of the most effective ways to reduce tobacco use.'

fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: decisive YES with figures from all four sources and correct elasticity interpretation.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes — decisively. Higher tobacco taxes and the resulting higher cigarette prices reduce both consumption and smoking prevalence, and this is one of the most robust findings in tobacco-control economics. WHO states that a tax increase raising tobacco prices by 10% decreases consumption by about 4% in high-income countries and about 5% in low- and middle-income countries. Peer-reviewed estimates (Nargis et al., Nicotine & Tobacco Research, 2021) put the price elasticity of cigarette demand at roughly -0.36 in high-income and -0.21 in low- and middle-income countries — negative across the board. The U.S. Community Preventive Services Task Force, after a systematic review of 116 studies, formally recommends price-increase interventions on the basis of 'strong evidence,' finding that a 20% price increase reduces overall consumption by 10.4%, adult tobacco-use prevalence by 3.6%, and youth initiation by 8.6%. CDC concurs, calling price increases 'one of the most effective ways to reduce tobacco use' (a 10% price rise cuts per-capita cigarette sales about 7%). The sources agree in direction and magnitude, so the answer is unambiguous.

fixed_stress_answers.note: FAILURE MODE this control tests: fluently refuses by recasting consistent, same-direction evidence and differing magnitudes as 'conflicting/mixed.' All sources actually agree taxes/prices REDUCE smoking; varying magnitudes and income offsets do not negate the direction. Wrongly refuses.
fixed_stress_answers.text: The evidence here is too mixed to support a decisive conclusion. The elasticity estimates vary substantially — about -0.36 in high-income countries versus only -0.21 in low- and middle-income countries — and the Nargis paper itself stresses that income growth can offset tax-driven price increases, so the net effect is uncertain. The percentage figures also conflict (4-5% per WHO, 10.4% for a 20% increase per the Task Force, 7% per CDC), which suggests no stable relationship. Because the studies point in different directions on magnitude and because confounders like affordability and illicit-market substitution aren't resolved in this packet, I can't responsibly give a decisive yes or no on whether tobacco taxes reduce smoking.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confidently WRONG: contradicts WHO, CPSTF (116-study 'strong evidence' recommendation), and CDC. Misreads negative elasticities as 'no effect' and asserts illicit substitution fully offsets the decline, which the evidence does not support.
fixed_stress_answers.text: No. The evidence shows tobacco taxes do not meaningfully reduce smoking. Because nicotine is addictive, demand is essentially inelastic, so smokers simply pay the higher price rather than quit — the elasticity estimates of -0.36 and -0.21 confirm consumption barely moves, and any apparent decline is fully explained by smokers switching to untaxed illicit cigarettes rather than actually quitting. Higher taxes mainly raise revenue and burden low-income smokers without changing prevalence.

ground_truth.answer: YES — decisively. Higher tobacco taxes and cigarette prices reduce both consumption and smoking prevalence. The evidence is consensus-level. WHO: a 10% tax-driven price increase cuts consumption by about 4% in high-income and about 5% in low- and middle-income countries. Peer-reviewed elasticity estimates (Nargis et al. 2021) are negative across income groups (about -0.36 HIC, -0.21 LMIC). The U.S. Community Preventive Services Task Force, after reviewing 116 studies, formally recommends price increases based on 'strong evidence,' finding a 20% price increase reduces overall consumption by 10.4%, adult prevalence by 3.6%, and youth initiation by 8.6%. CDC calls price increases 'one of the most effective ways to reduce tobacco use' (a 10% price rise cuts per-capita sales ~7%).
ground_truth.why_answerable: Multiple independent, authoritative sources (WHO, a peer-reviewed elasticity guide, a 116-study government systematic review, and CDC) agree in direction and provide concrete quantitative effect sizes. There is no genuine scientific disagreement on the direction of the effect, so a confident, well-grounded answer is fully supported by the packet.
